# [[Classic] SendAddonMessage problems](/en/wow/t/classic-sendaddonmessage-problems/620054)

Guides UI and Macro

[Rylak-3034442](https://us.forums.blizzard.com/en/wow/u/Rylak-3034442) (Rylak) August 26, 2020, 9:47am 2

I’ve experienced the same issue. What you’re seeing is the throttling that Blizzard implemented in mid-may to try to mitigate the amount of network traffic generated by threat addons.  
Since they didn’t have a means to reliably pull real time threat data about other raid members, they needed to communicate a large amount of data. Because of this, Blizzard enforced throttling and then in 1.13.5 they added the Threat API [ [source](https://us.forums.blizzard.com/en/wow/t/ptr-patch-notes-wow-classic-version-1135/553585) ].  
Unfortunately, they never withdrew the throttling.

From observing throttled behaviour, I can confirm the following:

* It is intermittent. It does not occur at the same time every day, nor does it necessarily occur every day.
* It is not occurring on all realms. I’m on Remulos-US and I’ve only experienced throttling a few times.
* C\_ChatInfo.SendAddonMessage has a return value - whether or not the message was successfully sent. During periods of throttling, this will return true regardless of whether or not it is being throttled.
* Recent changes to my code suggest that the whisper channel _may_ not be throttled. I haven’t experienced any issues with using that channel.
* + A quick note on this point - I don’t know how the backend of the messaging system operates, but the fact that I’m considering sending 40 messages via the whisper channel as opposed to 1 message via the raid channel… I’m lost for words.

Unfortunately, at this stage I can’t offer you a solution. I’m still trying to arrive at one myself. I only offer what I know and hope that it might be able to help you.

Guides UI and Macro

[Cruciformer-539871](https://us.forums.blizzard.com/en/wow/u/Cruciformer-539871) (Cruciformer) August 23, 2020, 2:44pm 1

I am the author of a popular suicide kings loot distribution mod. It’s been around since BC up until ML was removed, and revived for Classic WoW.

Since about 1.13.3 C\_ChatInfo.SendAddonMessage() has been broken. My mod relied on the ability to send the config to all raid users, about 3-4K of data. I have done all the usual things to mitigate the server flood tripwire, such as using the latest AceComm and ChatThrottleLib, but things are still failing. Even with CTL messages are silently ignored if they come too fast. Which given CTL’s sole reason for existence, shouldn’t be happening.

I suspect this was a change introduced when Blizzard was clamping down on using channels.
I do not think CTL itself is at fault as the API seems to accept data with no indication of failure, and then randomly decide not to deliver any of the messages, or just some, which is even worse.

This will be extremely difficult to work around. I am happy to provide any additional information should it be required, and to test.

[Cruciformer-539871](https://us.forums.blizzard.com/en/wow/u/Cruciformer-539871) (Cruciformer) August 26, 2020, 10:03pm 3

There was a bit of discussion about this on WoWUIDev and the immediate answer is, simply: send less data. Not the answer I would have preferred but it is valid. However the problem comes when even after a developer really does do everything possible to minimise the payload, there will come a point where even that runs into the throttle.

I understand the reasons behind the current throttle but I think a lot (if not all) of the problems they were trying to solve have no gone away and the throttle rates could be better tuned.

All I can hope for is that someone from Blizzard, or someone with influence that can talk to someone at Blizzard, and get them to rethink / retune the throttle mechanism a little bit.
And I will do what I can to further reduce the payload size in my mod.

results.title: The Thundering Herd Problem (and How to Actually Fix It) - DEV Community
excerpts:
It happens when a large number of processes or requests are woken up at the same time to compete for the same limited resource, and only one (or a few) of them actually needed to do the work.

Picture a stadium after the final whistle. Everyone stands up at once and rushes toward the same exit door, even though there are three other doors nobody's using. The door isn't broken, it's just completely overwhelmed by everyone arriving at the exact same moment.

That's a thundering herd. Not too many requests, just too many requests hitting the same door at the same time.

##  Where it shows up in real systems

There are a few classic triggers:

* **Cache expiration** : a hot cache key (say, the homepage data) expires, and the next 10,000 requests all miss the cache simultaneously and slam the database trying to rebuild it.

...

They all boil down to the same underlying idea: **decouple the trigger from the reaction** , so a single event doesn't cause every consumer to act at the exact same instant.

|Scenario |Symptom |Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
|Cache expiration |DB spike on key miss |Request coalescing / singleflight |
|Cache expiration |Predictable, recurring spikes |Probabilistic early expiration |
|Worker wakeups |Wasted context switches |Exclusive wake / atomic job claim |
|Retry storms |Repeated synchronized retries |Backoff with jitter |

Short version: if a lot of things are reacting to one thing at the same time, add either **coordination** (only one of them should actually do the work) or **randomness** (spread the reaction out over time). Almost every thundering herd fix is one of those two ideas wearing a different costume.

results.title: Requests at Scale — Exponential Backoff with Jitter (with ...
excerpts:
Then it just makes the stampede happen at longer intervals.

That’s where **jitter** comes in.

Instead of everyone retrying at **exactly** 1s, 2s, 4s… you add a little randomness:

```
Retry after 1000ms + random(0–200ms)  
Retry after 2000ms + random(0–200ms)  
Retry after 4000ms + random(0–200ms)
```

So one client might retry at `1.03s` , another at `1.15s` , another at `1.19s` .

This randomness **spreads the load** , giving your server a chance to recover instead of getting hammered in unison.

Think of it like this:

* Without jitter, retrying clients act like a **marching band** — every horn blasting in perfect sync.
* With jitter, it’s more like a **crowd talking** — still noisy, but naturally staggered, distributed, so the system can keep up.

In practice, this means the server actually has time to **breathe** . While 1,000 clients might all retry _around_ `t=0` , only a few dozen hit it at any given moment — say, 50 at `t=1020ms` , a few at `t=1100ms` , and so on.

...

**Upper bounding by max (30s in our example)** means retries will _tend_ toward that ceiling without ever lockstepping.

At scale (millions of clients), **the law of large numbers wins** . Over many clients, some hit small numbers, some hit large, but the _distribution_ evens out.

So while one client _might_ get a weird 300ms retry, across millions of clients the system sees a _smooth spread_ — which is what the server cares about.

**Now compared to Equal Jitter:** Equal Jitter’s lower bound rises strictly, so everyone clusters around similar ranges, while Decorrelated Jitter “wanders” more — some retries are short, some long — which actually helps spread retries _better_ across clients, avoiding bursts.

Decorrelated Jitter is the recommended strategy for implementing Jitter. It has been found to be the smoothest under real-world network chaos.

Netflix/AWS tested it at scale and found it _reduced traffic spikes best_ while keeping retry latency reasonable.

...

Don’t let retries grow unbounded — it wastes time and ties up client resources. A max like **30 seconds** is a good rule of thumb.
2. **Add jitter intentionally.**  
   Even a small random offset (±100–300 ms) massively reduces the thundering-herd effect. It doesn’t always have to be fancy — just enough to keep clients from marching in sync.
3. **Backoff per request type.**  
   Not all operations are equal — a cheap GET can retry aggressively, but a payment or data-write shouldn’t. Use custom backoff logic when it matters.
4. **Combine with circuit breakers.**  
   If the service is really down, don’t keep hammering it. Stop retrying for a while and surface an error instead.
5. **Log retries.**  
   Track how often and how long retries happen — patterns here often reveal flaky dependencies or network issues.

## Some common gotchas to look out for

1. **“Retrying forever” loops.**  
   If a dependency’s default is to retry indefinitely, cap it manually.

results.title: The Thundering Herd Problem
excerpts:
A big sale event on **Amazon** or a product launch by **Apple**.
    
    ### What happens
    
    *   Traffic increases because **more users arrive**.
        
    *   Requests are **spread across time**.
        
    *   Caching and scaling usually help absorb it.
        

### Thundering Herd Spike

*   A **thundering herd** is a spike caused by **many clients reacting to the same event simultaneously**.
    
*   Example triggers:
    
    *   Cache expiry
        
    *   Lock release
        
    *   Service recovery
        
    *   Token expiration
        
    
    ### Example
    
    Cache expires in **Redis** and thousands of servers rebuild the same data.
    

| Feature | Normal Spike | Thundering Herd |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cause | More users | Same event triggers many clients |
| Request timing | Gradual | Simultaneous |
| Work duplication | Minimal | Very high |
| Predictability | Often predictable | Sudden |
| Example | Sale event traffic | Cache expiry storm |

...

*   Go’s singleflight library
    

### Distributed Locking

Ensure that **only one server rebuilds a resource** (like a cache entry). This prevents multiple servers from doing the same work.

![](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/678e83c68aa41bec2db0ff71/6becbf6b-d764-47fd-9f54-6ee394447e9e.png align="center")

### Randomized Cache Expiry (Jitter)

### Exponential Backoff with Jitter

When requests fail or timeout, clients retry. If everyone retries immediately, it creates a **retry storm**. so gradually increase retry delay

example: retry\_delay = base \* 2^attempt + random\_jitter

Retry 1 → 100 ms

Retry 2 → 200 ms

Retry 3 → 400 ms

Retry 4 → 800 ms

### Serve Stale Data (Stale-While-Revalidate)

Instead of forcing all requests to regenerate fresh data, Serve **slightly stale cache,** Refresh cache **in background**

Benefits:

*   Users still get fast responses
    
*   Database load stays low
